question_en: IFRS most likely permit lessees to report the:
option_a: entire lease payment as a cash outflow under operating activities.
option_b: reduction of lease liabilities as a cash outflow under investing activities.
option_c: interest portion of the lease payment as cash outflow under financing activities.
explanation_en:
Financial statement impact to the lessee
Governing standard Balance sheet Income statement Cash flow statement
Reduction of lease liability: CFF
IFRS: all leases Asset Depreciation Interest payments:
US GAAP: finance lease Liability Interest IFRS: CFF or CFO
US GAAP: CFO
Asset
US GAAP: operating lease Single expense item Entire lease payment: CFO
Liability
In a lease contract, the lessee makes periodic payments to the lessor for the right to use an asset for a specified amount of time. Under IFRS, all
leases are treated like asset purchases financed with borrowed funds. At inception, the lessee records a right-of-use asset and a lease liability
equal to the present value of the future lease payments.
After inception, periodic payments are separated into two categories:
A portion is applied toward reducing the lease liability principal and is recorded as a cash outflow under financing activities.
The rest of the monthly payment counts as interest and is recorded as a cash outflow under financing activities or operating activities.
Note that the interest portion of the lease payments is classified under financing or operating activities under IFRS but is strictly classified as
operating activities under US GAAP.
(Choice A) Under IFRS, the principal portion of the lease payment cannot be classified as an operating activity.
(Choice B) Under IFRS, the reduction of the lease liability is treated as a cash outflow from financing, not investing.

question_en: .A company reporting under US GAAP leases a factory building under a long-term operating lease contract. On the income statement, the ongoing expenses pertaining to the lease should most appropriately be reported:
option_a: in equal amounts each period, under a single line item.
option_b: in different amounts each period, under a single line item.
option_c: in different amounts each period, under depreciation expense and interest expense.
explanation_en:
Financial statement impact to the lessee
Governing standard Balance sheet Income statement Cash flow statement
Reduction of lease liability: CFF
IFRS: all leases Asset Depreciation Interest payments:
US GAAP: finance lease Liability Interest IFRS: CFF or CFO
US GAAP: CFO
Asset
US GAAP: operating lease Single expense item Entire lease payment: CFO
Liability
In a lease contract, the lessee makes periodic payments to the lessor for the right to use an asset for a specified amount of time. Under US
GAAP, long-term leases can be classified as finance or operating.
Operating leases are treated like a rental agreement. Each period, the lessee records on the income statement a single expense, which is
equal to the average periodic lease payment. For example, if a 10-year operating lease's total contractual amount is CAD 120 million, then the
monthly income statement expense will be CAD 1 million (or CAD 120 million / 120 months), regardless of the actual lease payments each month
(Choice B).
Finance leases are treated liked an asset purchase financed with borrowed funds. Each period, the lessee records on the income statement the
depreciation expense from the leased asset and the interest expense from the "debt."
(Choice C) In a finance lease, not an operating lease, the expense can be separated into depreciation expense and interest expense on the
income statement. Furthermore, interest expense is different each period.

question_en: A manufacturing company maintains a defined benefit plan for its employees who are directly involved in the manufacturing process. The company most appropriately recognizes contributions made for those employees:
option_a: immediately as a separate operating expense.
option_b: as a separate operating expense only when the employees retire.
option_c: as cost of goods sold when it sells goods that those employees made.
explanation_en:
Defined contribution plans (DC) Defined benefit plans (DB)
No future benefit guaranteed Employer promises future benefits
Employee bears responsibility for performance Employer bears responsibility for performance
Financial impact limited to expensing contributions made to Performance of plan assets can significantly impact
participants' accounts financial reporting
Accounting is straightforward and simple Accounting is complicated
No significant differences between US GAAP and IFRS Significant differences between US GAAP and IFRS
A defined benefit (DB) plan is a pension plan that guarantees employees income when they retire. The benefit for each employee is formula-
driven and can be based on several variables, including years of service and average compensation. To provide this benefit, employers contribute
an amount each year into one separate investment account that is maintained for the benefit of all employees.
DB plan contributions are deductible expenses, but IFRS and US GAAP treat pension contributions as a type of wage expense. Wage expenses
for employees in a direct production capacity, such as this company's manufacturing employees, are included as a cost of inventory.
Inventory costs are not expensed immediately. Instead, they are included in cost of goods sold (COGS) when the company sells the inventory.
(Choice A) Contributions to a DB plan are deductible when made. The company does not wait until the employee begins receiving pension
benefits to deduct prior contributions.
(Choice B) For a manufacturing company, pension contributions are included as wage expenses. Wage expenses for manufacturing employees
are included as part of inventory and expensed as COGS. Wage expenses for nonmanufacturing employees are part of selling, general and
administrative expenses. The company's footnotes to its financial statements provide more detail on the different components of wage expenses.

question_en: Under US GAAP, a lessee reports periodic payments for the second year of a finance lease. Compared to using an operating lease, the lessee will most likely report:
option_a: less cash flow from financing activities.
option_b: less cash flow from operating activities.
option_c: more cash flow from investing activities.
explanation_en:
Long-term leases under US GAAP: lessee's perspective
Type Balance sheet Income statement Cash flow statement
Reduction of lease liability:
Asset Depreciation
Finance lease ↓ CFF
Liability Interest
Interest payments: ↓ CFO
Asset
Operating lease Single expense Entire lease payment: ↓ CFO
Liability
In a long-term lease contract, the lessee makes periodic payments to the lessor for the right to use an asset (ie, right of use [ROU]) for a specified
period. Under US GAAP, long-term leases can be classified as finance or operating.
Finance leases are treated like asset purchases financed with borrowed funds (from the lessor). At inception, the lessee simultaneously records
an ROU asset and a lease liability, both equal to the present value of the future lease payments. After inception, a portion of each periodic
payment is applied toward reducing the liability (ie, principal reduction), which reduces cash from financing activities. Therefore, cash flow
from financing (CFF) is less under a finance lease. The rest of the monthly payment counts as interest and reduces cash from operating
activities (CFO).
Operating leases are treated like rental agreements. In each period, the entire periodic payment is treated like rent expense and reduces cash
from operating activities on the cash flow statement. Therefore, CFO under an operating lease is less than CFO under a finance lease (Choice
B).
(Choice C) After inception, periodic payments do not affect cash flows from investing activities regardless of lease type.

subtopic: 5.08 Topics in Long-Term Liabilities and Equity
question_en: A company issued coupon-paying bonds with a face value of £5 million. It used the proceeds to purchase one of its suppliers. The company uses IFRS for financial reporting. In its statement of cash flows, it can report its coupon payments on the bonds as:
option_a: cash from financing (CFF) or cash from investing (CFI).
option_b: cash from investing (CFI) or cash from operations (CFO).
option_c: cash from financing (CFF) or cash from operations (CFO).
explanation_en:
Cash flows consist of both outflows and inflows. From an issuer's (ie, borrower's) perspective, the proceeds from issuing a bond are a cash inflow,
whereas interest and principal payments on the bond are outflows. Both GAAP and IFRS classify receipt and payment of bond principal as cash
from financing (CFF). US GAAP classify all interest payments (ie, outflows) as cash from operations (CFO), but IFRS permit companies to
classify those payments as either CFO or CFF.
Owning another company's bonds is an investment. Interest received on those bonds is directly linked to that investment, so IFRS allow interest
received to be classified as cash from investing (CFI). However, this does not apply to interest paid on debt, even if the borrower uses the
proceeds from the bond for an investment, as in this case. Interest paid is either CFO or CFF, but never CFI, so (Choices A and B) are incorrect.

question_en: A company has a defined contribution pension plan and reports under IFRS. Which of the following items relating to the plan's participant accounts are most likely to be disclosed on the company's income statement?
option_a: Gains or losses on plan investments
option_b: Company contributions made to participants' accounts
option_c: Interest and dividends earned and paid on plan investments
explanation_en:
Defined contribution plans (DC) Defined benefit plans (DB)
No future benefit guaranteed Employer promises future benefits
Employee bears responsibility for performance Employer bears responsibility for performance
Financial impact limited to expensing contributions made to Performance of plan assets can significantly impact
participants' accounts financial reporting
Accounting is straightforward and simple Accounting is complicated
No significant differences between US GAAP and IFRS Significant differences between US GAAP and IFRS
A defined contribution (DC) plan is a type of employee retirement plan. Unlike a defined benefit (DB) plan, a DC plan does not guarantee the
employee any benefit at retirement. Instead, the employer establishes the plan and selects diverse investments that participants (ie, employees)
can invest in, allocating their account balance based on their individual risk and return preferences.
The funding in a DC plan can be contributions from the employer, the participant's own contributions (ie, salary deferrals), or a combination of
these. In all cases, the participant, not the employer, is responsible for the account's performance. All investment gains or losses, as well as
dividend or interest income generated by those investments, benefit the participant, not the employer (Choices A and C).
An employer receives a tax deduction for any contributions that it makes to participants' accounts. Deductibility applies whether the contributions
are contractually required (eg, collective bargaining agreements) or voluntary (eg, profit-sharing plans).

question_en: After entering a finance lease agreement, the lessor most appropriately records periodic:
explanation_en:
Financial statement impact on the lessor
Balance sheet Income statement Cash flow statement
Remove leased asset Record interest revenue Lease payments received: CFO
Finance lease Recognize lease receivable
Record gain or loss
Retains leased asset Record lease income Lease payments received: CFO
Operating lease
Record depreciation
CFO = cash flow from operating activities, CFI = cash flow from financing activities
In a lease contract, the lessor grants the lessee the right to use an asset over a specific period of time in exchange for scheduled regular
payments. For accounting purposes, most leases are classified as finance leases, although some exceptions (eg, airport terminals) are treated as
operating leases.
From a lessor's perspective, a finance lease is economically equivalent to financing an asset sale to the lessee (customer). At inception of the
lease, the lessor removes the leased asset from its balance sheet and simultaneously records a receivable. Subsequently, the lessor reports
interest revenue earned from the financing provided to the customer.
In contrast, operating leases are treated like rental agreements. The lessor retains the asset at inception and subsequently records rental (ie,
lease) income and depreciation (Choices A and C).

question_en:
This fiscal year, a company:

- received in advance from a customer $60,000 for goods to be delivered next year. This amount is recognized as revenue for tax purposes this year but cannot be recognized as accounting revenue until next year.
- prepaid a vendor $12,000 for monthly office cleaning services that will begin next year. This amount cannot be recognized as an accounting expense until next year but is deductible for tax purposes this year.

Based on only this information, if the company is subject to a 25% tax rate, then this year it most likely will experience a:
explanation_en: Deferred tax asset vs. deferred tax liability Item created Accounting reporting Tax reporting Deferred tax asset1 Income tax expense < Taxes payable Deferred tax liability2 Income tax expense > Taxes payable 1Overpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax asset 2Underpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax liability Deferred tax assets (DTA) and liabilities (DTL) arise from temporary differences between income tax expense and taxes payable for a period. Income tax expense is based on pretax income from the income statement and is reported for financial reporting (accounting) purposes. Taxes payable is based on taxable income on the tax return and is the actual amount owed to the government. In this scenario, the company has greater taxes payable ($12,000) than income tax expense ($0) for the period. This temporary "overpayment" leads to a $12,000 increase in DTA, which is expected to reverse in a future period when the respective revenues and expenses are recognized for accounting purposes (Choice B). (Choice C) A $48,000 increase in DTA results from incorrectly taking the difference between taxable income and pretax income.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en: In 20X8, a security company received payment of £20,000 for services that it will not perform until 20X9. If the statutory tax rate increases from 25% to 30% in 20X9, the effect of this advance payment in 20X9 most likely causes an increase in:
explanation_en: Deferred tax assets (DTA) arise when a company's taxable income temporarily exceeds its pretax income. The imbalance causes the company to pay more in taxes than it reports as tax expense on its income statement. This occurs when the company pays tax on cash it receives in the current period but for which it will not earn and recognize as revenue until a future period. The carrying value and tax base of an item are similar concepts. Carrying value refers to an item's value that the company reports in its financial reporting. The tax base is the value that the company uses for the same item when it calculates its tax obligations. The company pays tax on the advance payment in 20X8, even though it does not recognize the cash as revenue in 20X8 since it has not performed the agreed-upon services. It creates a liability (eg, deferred revenue) of £20,000 to account for the cash, and the liability's 20X8 carrying value is £20,000. The cash's 20X8 tax base equals zero since it was taxed when received in 20X8. This difference results in a DTA. A DTA is the difference between the item's carrying value and its tax base, multiplied by the tax rate: (20,000 − 0) × 25% = £5,000. When the tax rate increases to 30% in 20X9, the DTA also increases: (20,000 − 0) × 30% = £6,000, an increase of £1,000. (Choice A) The increase in DTA from £5,000 to £6,000 causes tax expense to decline, not increase, by £1,000. (Choice B) The company paid the tax on the customer advance in 20X8, so that has no impact on its tax obligations for 20X9.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en: An appliance manufacturing company depreciates its noncurrent assets for financial reporting using straight-line depreciation, but the tax code permits the company to use accelerated depreciation for tax purposes. If this company acquired an asset this year that cost €3 million, has a three-year useful life, and has zero salvage value, the most likely impact on the company's financial statements at the end of this year will be that the tax base of the asset is:
explanation_en: Deferred tax liabilities (DTLs) arise when a company's pretax income temporarily exceeds its taxable income. For example, when a company uses accelerated depreciation for taxes and straight-line depreciation for financial reporting in the early years of the life of the deferred tax asset (DTA), taxable income is lower than pretax income due to the higher depreciation expense. The difference between pretax income and taxable income is temporary and reverses as the asset is fully depreciated. A DTL represents future taxes. When the statutory tax rate decreases, the DTL decreases since the delayed taxable event will now be taxed at the lower rate and the company will owe less tax in the future (Choice C). (Choice A) The DTA will also decrease if tax rates decrease, since it becomes less valuable as an offset for future taxes when those taxes are less.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company has a deferred tax asset (DTA) and a deferred tax liability (DTL). If tax rates fall during the next year, holding all else equal, it is most likely that the company's deferred tax:
explanation_en: An asset's carrying amount reflects the reported book value on the balance sheet (per accounting standards). An asset's tax base reflects the value that remains as a deductible expense (per the tax code) over the asset's useful life. Differences between accounting standards and tax codes may cause carrying amounts and tax bases to differ, which may lead to deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities. In this scenario, calculate each asset's amount and tax base to determine the total difference in 20X5: Investment securities are valued at €200,000 for accounting purposes and €190,000 for tax purposes. For the €1 million of capitalized software development costs, 20% is amortized for accounting purposes, so the carrying amount is €800,000 [(1 − 0.2) × 1 million]. In comparison, 25% is amortized for tax purposes, so the tax base is €750,000 [(1 − 0.25) × 1 million]. For (net) accounts receivable (AR), €480,000 is recorded on the balance sheet based on an accounting estimate of €20,000 for allowance for doubtful accounts. Therefore, the gross AR must be €500,000. For tax purposes, the allowance for doubtful accounts is calculated as 10% of €500,000 in gross AR, or €50,000. Therefore, the tax base for net AR is €450,000 (500,000 − 50,000). In aggregate, the carrying amount of assets is €90,000 more than the tax base. (Choice A) €27,000 is the deferred tax liability, which is the product of €90,000 and the 30% tax rate. (Choice C) €108,000 results from misapplying the 10% to the carrying amount of net AR (€480,000), when it should be applied to the gross AR amount of €500,000.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company purchases a service on credit for TRY 10,000 in 20X8. The company recognizes the expense on its income statement that year but will not pay cash until 20X9. Tax laws require that the company recognize the expense when cash is paid. If the company's tax rate is 30%, in 20X8 the company would most appropriately record a:
explanation_en: Deferred tax assets (DTA) and deferred tax liabilities (DTL) arise from temporary differences between pretax income and taxable income. Compensation in stock is a deductible expense, and for financial reporting, the company deducts the market value of the shares in the period that it accrues the expense. The company will deduct the value of the shares for tax purposes in the future period when it delivers the shares. The lack of tax deductibility in the current period means that the company pays more taxes than it reports as tax expenses. This is a temporary difference since the company will pay less tax in the period of delivery than it pays in the current period. To account for the difference, the company creates a DTA. This advises investors and analysts that the discrepancy between what the company pays in tax currently and what it reports as tax expense will reverse in a future period. When the discrepancy is permanent (ie, will never reverse), no deferred tax item is created. The chart below shows items that lead to permanent differences: Major areas resulting in permanent differences between pretax and taxable income Item Impact Reason Interest on state and local Pretax income > taxable Interest is tax-free government bonds income Fines and penalties Fines are tax-deductible Taxable income > pretax Certain entertainment expenses Not all are fully tax-deductible income Certain benefits for senior Some benefits, such as company-paid premiums on life insurance, management are not tax-deductible Companies include interest on municipal (state and local) bonds as revenue for financial reporting, but municipal bond interest is never taxable to the recipient (Choice A). Similarly, fines imposed by a government agency are deducted as an operating expense for financial reporting, but fines cannot be deducted when calculating taxable income (Choice C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en: A French catering firm prepares and supplies in-flight meals and snacks to airlines at various airports in Europe and reports its financial results under IFRS. Its tax rate is 25%. On January 1, 20X8, the firm incurred €800,000 in research costs to improve the efficiency of its operations. It expensed the entire amount on its income statement but recorded it as an asset for tax purposes. It will amortize this amount equally over four years. Which of the following is the most likely impact of the research costs on the firm's 20X8 financial results?
option_a: The research costs' carrying value equals €600,000.
option_b: The firm's taxable income is less than its pretax income.
option_c: The firm reports a deferred tax asset (DTA) of €150,000.
explanation_en: Deferred tax asset vs. deferred tax liability Income tax expense < taxes payable Deferred tax asset Created by overpaying tax in current period Income tax expense > taxes payable Deferred tax liability Created by underpaying tax in current period Deferred tax assets (DTAs) and deferred tax liabilities (DTLs) arise from differences between income tax expense and taxes payable for a period. Income tax expense is based on pretax income shown on the income statement for financial reporting (ie, accounting) purposes. Taxes payable are based on taxable income according to the tax code and reported on the tax return as the actual amount owed to the government. A DTL is incurred when income tax expense is greater than taxes payable, so the company pays less in taxes for the current year than it reports as income tax expense. This temporary "underpayment" generates a DTL that is expected to reverse later. In this question, assume revenue this year is $100,000. The $25,000 paid to the vendor (ie, prepaid expense) is recognized for tax purposes as a cash expense this year. However, for accounting purposes, the expense will not be reported until next year. This temporarily causes pretax income to be $25,000 more than taxable income, which creates a DTL of $5,000. (Choice A) A DTA is created when tax expense is less than tax payable. (Choice B) A valuation allowance account is a contra account to DTAs. It is recorded when certain amounts of DTAs are unlikely to be recovered in the future.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en: A deferred tax asset most likely results when:
option_a: taxable income is less than pretax income.
option_b: income tax expense is less than taxes payable.
option_c: income tax expense is greater than taxes payable.
explanation_en: Deferred tax asset vs. deferred tax liability Item created Accounting reporting Tax reporting Deferred tax asset1 Income tax expense < Taxes payable Deferred tax liability2 Income tax expense > Taxes payable 1Overpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax asset 2Underpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax liability A deferred tax asset is created when income tax expense is less than taxes payable. This means that the company pays more taxes for the current year (as shown on its tax return) than it reports as income tax expense (on its income statement). This temporary overpayment generates a future tax benefit (ie, deferred tax asset) since this difference is expected to reverse. For example, if the company receives $50,000 in cash before delivering services and the company's tax rate is 20%, then the result is as follows: Since the cash received from the customer (ie, unearned revenue) is recognized as revenue for tax purposes but not for accounting purposes, taxable income is greater than pretax income (ie, accounting profit) and taxes payable is greater than tax expense, which generates a deferred tax asset. (Choice A) Tax base refers to the value of an asset or liability for tax purposes. (Choice C) A deferred tax liability is created when deferred tax expense is more than taxes payable.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en: An increase in the statutory tax rate will most likely:
option_a: increase both deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities.
option_b: increase deferred tax assets and decrease deferred tax liabilities.
option_c: decrease deferred tax assets and increase deferred tax liabilities.
explanation_en: Tax laws allow companies to use different methods to report balance sheet items (eg, assets or liabilities) for tax purposes and financial reporting. Different reporting methods create temporary differences between an item's carrying value and its tax base. The tax base is the value of the asset for tax purposes. For financial reporting purposes, carrying value is the same as the asset's net book value. When an asset's carrying value exceeds its tax base, it indicates that reporting differences have resulted in a deferred tax liability (DTL). For example, if a company chooses to depreciate assets more rapidly for tax purposes than for financial reporting, then for tax reporting: depreciation expense is higher, taxable income is lower, tax expense is lower, taxes payable is lower, and tax base is lower than carrying value. DTL is temporary since under either method an asset's net cost fully depreciates over time. Due to the difference in depreciation methods, the company pays less now but owes future taxes; this debt is recorded as a DTL. (Choices A) Changes in equity valuation have no impact on deferred tax assets or liabilities. (Choices C) If a liability's carrying value is less than its tax base, it indicates use of a DTL.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en:
In 20X5, a company reports different asset amounts for accounting purposes and tax purposes:

- The company reports investment securities at fair value at €200,000 on the balance sheet. For tax purposes, the investments are valued at the original cost of €190,000.
- The company capitalizes €1 million in software development costs. For accounting purposes, 20% of the costs are amortized in 20X5. For tax purposes, 25% of the costs are amortized in 20X5.
- The company reports net accounts receivable (AR) of €480,000 after subtracting €20,000 in allowance for doubtful accounts. For tax purposes, the allowance for doubtful accounts is determined to be 10% of gross AR.

The statutory tax rate is 30%.

Based on this information, in 20X5 the carrying amount for assets exceeds the tax base by:
explanation_en: A deferred tax liability (DTL) is created when income tax expense (for financial reporting) temporarily exceeds taxes payable (for tax reporting) in a reporting period. This means that the company pays less taxes in the current period than it reports on its income statement. Therefore, this temporary "underpayment" generates a DTL that is expected to reverse in a future period. For example, a company may generate a DTL by reporting unrealized gains from holding certain securities on the income statement, but delaying recognition of gains for tax purposes until the securities are sold in a future period. When the securities are sold in the future, the company will report the realized gain as taxable income and reverse the liability. Sometimes a DTL is no longer expected to reverse in the future. For example, the company may decide to not sell the security and instead own it indefinitely. When this happens, the company should write off the DTL and increase shareholders' equity by the same amount. (Choice A) There is no change in total assets. Total assets equal liabilities plus equity. In this scenario, the decrease in the DTL is fully offset by the increase in shareholders' equity. (Choice B) Taxable income is determined by taxable revenues and allowed expenses. It is not determined by changes to DTL.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following items is most likely to result in the creation of a deferred tax item?
option_a: Interest received on city and state government bonds
option_b: Compensation paid in the future with shares of company stock
option_c: Fines paid to a government agency to settle violations of security laws
explanation_en: Deferred tax asset vs. deferred tax liability Item created Accounting reporting Tax reporting Deferred tax asset1 Income tax expense < Taxes payable Deferred tax liability2 Income tax expense > Taxes payable 1Overpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax asset 2Underpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax liability Deferred taxes account for temporary differences between income tax expense and taxes payable. Such differences occur due to differences between tax reporting and financial reporting. A deferred tax liability (DTL) is created when a company pays less tax (tax reporting) than it reports on its income statement (financial reporting); the DTL represents future taxes payable. While current taxes payable are based on the tax rates that apply on the balance sheet date, a DTL is measured by tax rates that are expected to be in place at the time of the liability's settlement. If expected rates are higher or lower than existing rates, that will be reflected in the value of the DTL. This provides a more realistic measure of value since it is based on future rates, not historical ones (eg, balance sheet date, average over the fiscal year) (Choices A and B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.09 Analysis of Income Taxes - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company has a tax rate of 25% and reports an income tax expense of CAD 100 million and taxes payable of CAD 75 million for the current year. If this difference is due solely to using different depreciation methods for financial reporting and tax purposes, the company most likely has a:
explanation_en: Deferred tax assets (DTAs) and deferred tax liabilities (DTLs) reflect temporary differences between income tax expense and taxes payable for a period. Such differences are created by differences between accounting standards and tax laws. Income tax expense is reported on the income statement according to accounting standards, whereas taxes payable is the actual amount owed to the government (based on applicable tax laws). When tax expense is greater than taxes payable, a DTL is created since the company pays less in taxes in the current period but will owe more in taxes in the future. When tax expense is less than taxes payable, a DTA is created since the company pays more in taxes in the current period and will owe less in taxes in the future. The equation above shows how the changes in DTL and DTA are related to tax expense and taxes payable. To calculate the change in DTL in this scenario, substitute values for all the other variables. (Choice A) A ¥4 million increase results from placing the incorrect sign in front of ΔDTA. (Choice C) A ¥10 million decrease results from placing the incorrect sign in front of ΔDTL.

explanation_en: Comparison of deferred tax assets (DTA) and liabilities (DTL) DTA DTL Temporary Taxable income > accounting income Taxable income < accounting income differences Future tax Decrease Increase obligations Revaluation Change value if future earnings are at risk None Accelerated for financial reporting; straight-line for tax Straight-line for financial reporting; accelerated for tax Depreciation reporting reporting Expenses Expenses recorded before cash is paid Expenses recorded after cash is paid Carryforwards Prior years' losses None Revenue Cash received before revenue is earned Cash received after revenue is earned A deferred tax asset (DTA) is created when a company's accounting income is less than its taxable income. In that case, according to the tax code, the tax expense that the company must pay is greater than its income tax expense based on financial reporting. Often, these differences arise when the tax code and accounting standards differ on how and when companies should recognize revenues and expenses. A DTA is temporary since its benefit is expected to offset future taxes. For example, accounting income is less than taxable income when a company elects accelerated depreciation for financial reporting and straight- line depreciation for tax reporting. Using straight-line depreciation for tax reporting results in lower depreciation expense and higher taxable income than when it is used for financial reporting. Higher taxable income increases tax expense and taxes payable. Overpayment of tax today results in a DTA since the company will pay less tax in the future. (Choice A) Carryforwards of prior years' losses, not gains, may be used against future gains and are recorded as DTAs. Under most tax laws, gains are immediately taxable and are usually disallowed as carryforwards. (Choice C) Foreign or domestic currency received for revenue earned during the same period creates neither a DTA nor a deferred tax liability since accounting standards and the tax code recognize the currency as income.

question_en: A company recognizes all anticipated payments from an installment sale as revenue in the current period for accounting purposes. The tax code only taxes payments that the company receives. In the current period, for the installment sale revenue, the company most appropriately records:
option_c: neither a deferred tax asset nor a deferred tax liability.
explanation_en: Deferred tax assets (DTA) and liabilities arise from temporary differences between income tax expense and taxes payable for a period. These differences are expected to reverse over time and offset previous deferred tax items. Income tax expense is based on reported accounting income from the income statement. Taxes payable is based on taxable income on the tax return and is the actual amount owed to the government. DTA arise when: Taxable income > Accounting income and Taxes payable > Tax expense. Deferred tax liabilities (DTL) arise when: Taxable income < Accounting income and Taxes payable < Tax expense. In this scenario, a DTA is created since taxable income is greater than accounting income (Choice C). The deferred tax amount can be calculated as the product of the absolute difference between the taxable income and accounting income and the tax rate. Therefore, the size of the deferred tax item is directly correlated to the tax rate. If the tax rate were higher, the amount of the DTA increase would be higher as well (Choice A).
